newsitem.title: USA: Ship captain says siren kept crew from hearing orders.
newsitem.headline: Ship captain says siren kept crew from hearing orders.

text.p: The Chinese captain of a freighter that crashed into a crowded riverfront shopping mall said on Wednesday the ship's emergency warning sirens kept his crew from hearing some of his commands.

Jing Kuan Deng, skipper of the Liberian-flagged Bright Field, was testifying on the second day of a Coast Guard Board of Investigation into the accident, held jointly with National Transportation Safety Board investigators and a representative of Liberia.

National Transportation Safety Board investigator John Hammerschmidt said the freighter rammed the wharf after its main oil pump lost pressure, which tripped an automatic control system that reduced the engines' speed along with the ship's manoeuvrability, putting it at the mercy of powerful river currents.
At least 116 people were injured, most of them as they attempted to flee from the scene.
Although Deng spoke only through interpreters, he appeared to understand some of the questions asked in English and began answering before the interpreter completed the translation.
Deng said he asked the engine room by radio to explain the ship's reduced speed and ordered them to increase it to boost manoeuvrability.
He said the marine emergency warning siren, five quick blasts, repeated, kept some of his crew from hearing his orders, including one to "let go port anchor."

Deng said he tried to use body motions to get the attention of the crew member by the anchor, and eventually established radio contact, but the communications were broken up and hard to understand because of the siren blasts.
On Tuesday river pilot Ted Davisson testified he got no response from the captain after ordering a hard turn to the right and dropped anchors, and was not sure the orders were followed.

Although river pilots are responsible for safely navigating the treacherous Mississippi River currents through New Orleans to the mouth of the river, ultimate authority over the crew and ship remains with the captain.
